title: It Doesn't Matter: The Non-Utility of Medication in Childhood Behavior Disorders?
subtitle: A surprising new study compared medication vs medication free treatment and found absolutely no difference.
body_html:
When it comes to the epidemiology of healthcare, thank God for Northern Europe. Countries like Finland and The Netherlands, have national health systems that allow for extremely robust science at a population level. Now, it's pretty easy to argue that places that are not Northern Europe are different from Northern Europe, and make snarky comments about generalizability. However, it's not like we have large scale data from a vast array of other entire countries on the health outcomes across the entire populations to choose from.

Therefore, a lot of the world’s large scale epidemiological and cost-effectiveness data comes from this part of the world.

Today's article is about a surprising study. Not every study shows something is different. Some studies failed to reject the null hypothesis. This means there's no difference between condition A and condition B. Usually, in an experimental design, this is because the drug or intervention doesn't work for the condition being studied. In order to keep you reading, here's a picture of my daughter who probably has ADHD, because her dad has ADHD, and this is a highly heritable condition.

It's always a bit more surprising when we get a result that shows no difference between things that have many studies showing that in more carefully controlled settings there is a difference.

This paper looked at 209 kids who were Dutch. These young people were treated, in their communities, either with a medication free approach to their behavioral disorder, which all of them had, or with a combination of medications and other treatments. Previous studies, the landmark MTA trial, demonstrated that behavioral treatments were inferior to oral medication's in the treatment of ADHD, but that study wasn't specifically including oppositional define disorder in the data set. It was designed to show that a very high-quality behavioral treatment was just as good as methylphenidate, and it was actually stopped in the middle of the study. So the study, with its negative result, challenges orthodoxy, even while it asks a different question about a similar population.

Share

And given I've already, you're not gonna be surprised to hear there wasn't no difference. But it wasn't just there was no difference in terms of outcomes. There was no difference in terms of … anything. There was no difference in terms of cost-effectiveness. There was no difference in terms of quality of life. There was no difference in terms of impairment in the life of the child. It literally didn't matter at all, other than side effects, which are not meaningfully addressed in this paper. No, although this is an observational study, it's not retrospective, it's prospective. Thus the Sample Size is not thousands or millions, it's 100s, but they're closely followed. Here is the thrilling title of the paper:

Let’s dig into the paper. In the process, we're gonna learn a little bit about how to deal with missing data and cost-effectiveness studies, in case you ever needed to know how to do that.

Methods (Abstract):

Parents of 209 children (aged 5–12) who were referred to 1 of 10 Dutch youth mental healthcare institutions and who received treatment with (n = 108) or without (n = 101) the use of medication, filled out questionnaires at three timepoints (baseline, and ~ 6 and ~12 months later). Propensity score matching was used to make both groups comparable. Outcomes included quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), ADHD and ODD symptom severity, and impairment. Costs were measured from a societal perspective. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) were estimated, and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs) were derived to show uncertainty around the ICER.

Importantly, the children included in the perspective data collection of this observational trial were included at the very first hint of trouble:

We aimed to include participants before they received any treatment, therefore, a specific diagnosis was not a requirement for participation in the study. Instead, inclusion in the study was based on whether parents reported that their child was referred to a youth mental healthcare institution with inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, or behavioural problems, rather than a specific diagnosis.

Now, importantly, these groups were not randomized. We can't determine causality based on these data. We could think that parents who chose non-medication treatments have less sick children, and were making choices around medication or non-medication treatment based on severity. We are plausibly looking at two different groups.

Treatment and reference groups were constructed based on questionnaire responses from parents at T1 and/or T2 regarding treatments initiated since the start of the care trajectory. We created a ‘treatment group’ which consisted of children who had initiated medication treatment only or medication combined with other non-medication treatments. The comparator group consisted of children whose parents did not indicate medication treatment initiation during the care trajectory. We will refer to these groups as treatment with medication and treatment without medication groups, respectively.

We will look through the data together to determine is if we can ascertain whether these groups are different, or whether the groups are not significantly different, despite the lack of randomization. It is the authors job to convince us that the groups are pretty similar, so we will have a meaningful conclusions from their years of diligent work.

How Did They Count Costs?

They did not include every possible cost. They include the cost of medications. They didn't include the cost of taking your kid back-and-forth to therapy, which was present in both groups:

Only costs of medication were included, costs related to picking up prescriptions were not assessed. Costs related to travel to and from providers were not included in the cost estimation, as we did not have information on the distance to providers and modes of transportation to each of the services considered in this study.

They use some math on salaries in the Netherlands to estimate the cost of loss parental work. They did their best to figure out the overall burden of these treatments, but they couldn't count everything. It probably cost more than they are highlighting at the end of the day.

My favorite somewhat humorous moment in his paper is when they declined to count the cost of leisure time:

Opportunity costs for parents' and children's leisure time were not included in the analyses, as there is, to the best of our knowledge, no consensus on how to value this. Monetary valuations of leisure time can be considered arbitrary and can lead to a double-count (Hakkaart-van Roijen et al., 2016).

My children would likely have much stronger opinions about the opportunity cost of their leisure time, and I'm just gonna illustrate that next, with a cute picture. He is Quinn with an antique Katana.

Trent also takes a turn. This is a toy sword, however.

Were the Groups the Same at Baseline?

Our excellent friend Table One is a good place to start to determine if the two groups in the study might be different at baseline?

I have written about table one in a bunch of other articles, so if you go to the search bar, and you search “table one” you'll be able to see a series of articles that teach you how to read these things.

Looking at table one, because this is not a random sample, we're not looking to see if the randomization succeeded. We are looking to see if these groups are different at baseline, and you're going to notice something, they present the data twice.

What's this? We're gonna have to dig in a little deeper, raw data on the left, and something called multiply imputed and matched data on the right? Because at first, it looks like the groups are pretty different. The authors make it clear there's a lot of missing data at this point. They chose to not “raw dog” their data —that is a long flight joke. I’m on a plane from Tokyo to Newark with small children.

This is some sort of cost-effectiveness science witchcraft, isn't it?

Yes, yes it is. Raw data has some missing information in it. Maybe one group of parents didn't fill out six months or another group of parents failed to fill out the one year data? You could worry that these groups might be different. If investigators ignore the people who didn't collect all data, and use something simplistic to deal with that missing data problem, you could bias the results—very diligent patents might have had less distracting children, for example.

Multiple imputation is a way to create a set of model theoretical data sets to fill in the missing data in the real data set.

The authors used this approach to fill in the holes, and press the change out, if we take a look at that table one again, and look at the multiple imputation over on the right, we will see the groups look very similar when we appropriately address missing data:

We noticed something come up as a difference —which is that parents who previously had their children treated with medication were more likely to have their children treat with medication a second time— in this study. This is not a surprising result. The no med group was also slightly “less expensive” at baseline.

Thanks for joining me for that methodological deep dive, now, let's look at what happened. Parents chose to either treat their children with medication or treat their children without medication.

In oppositional defiant disorder and ADHD, mostly this means stimulant medications would've been used, particularly in the Netherlands. These are first line treatments.

What Were the Outcomes?

To drive this point home, I annotated this table:

And here we go again…

Do you have it, treatment was relatively cost-ineffective (77k/QALY)—the usual threshold for a success in cost-effectiveness research is 50,000k/QALY. However, it didn't matter if the treatment included oral medicine or did not.

The real world is messy, and it’s hard to get even excellent treatments to perform well once they hit the complex world of our real lives.

We need better treatments and psychosocial supports for families struggling with ADHD and ODD in their children.
